Escape velocity is the velocity at which an object can overpower gravity. The speed at which the kinetic energy of an object is equal to its gravitational potential energy is:
1/2mv^2 = GMm/r
where:
m = mass of gas molecule
M = mass of moon 7.34767E22 kg
G = Gravitational Constant = 6.67384E-11
r = distance between centers of mass = 1737400 m (radius of the Moon)
So, solving for v we get:
v = SQRT(2GM/r)
Any velocity in excess of that velocity will be sufficient for escape.
If we plug in the values for the moon we get an escape velocity of:
v = 2375.2 m/s (for comparison, Earth's is 11.2 km/s)
So, any gas molecule that happens to be flying upwards at greater that 2375.2 m/s will escape the moon and not return.
That leaves the question of how fast do gas molecules travel? We can calculate that using:
v = SQRT(3*R*T/M)
where:
R = 8.3141 J/kmol
T = temperature in Kelvin (298K is room temperature)
M = molecular weight of the gas
For air we get 506.6 m/s. For hydrogen we get 1927.8 m/s.
Those are average values. Some molecules will be going slower, some will be going faster. The speed of molecules changes as they gain or lose energy from thermal influences or collisions. We can see that any hydrogen the moon had would have left pretty quickly. Over time pretty much everything left. Technically the moon has an atmosphere but it is extremely thin and largely composed of gas that has recently escaped the soil.
